edges.relationship: Higham uses Hofstadter’s The Age of Reform as a specific example of how postwar historians revised the relationship between reform movements and historical change.
edges.evidence_note: The1959 paragraph beginning For one thing identifies Hofstadter’s influential1955 book, contrasts its treatment of Populism/Progressivism with its account of the New Deal, and uses this as evidence for changed periodization. This is a bounded historiographical resource, not proof Higham adopted every interpretation or equated Hofstadter with Boorstin’s approving conservatism. His paragraph notes the paradox of recognizing radical recent change; the principal extended criticism targets Boorstin. Hofstadter’s book itself unread.

edges.relationship: Higham argues that the Progressive framework associated jointly with Turner, Beard and Parrington absorbed social-conflict themes while its national assumptions constrained American historians’ engagement with Marxism.
edges.evidence_note: Own1989 argument462–463 names all three and assigns Beard the leading role in adapting social conflict; Turner is one member of the criticized collective, not sole originator. Higham distinguishes Progressive nationalism from Marxist internationalism and argues their appeal helped marginalize Marxism. His1959 appreciation of earlier moral engagement and institutional revision remains; this later specific criticism is not inferred from the broad existing field edge1472. Turner’s own work unread.

edges.relationship: Higham explicitly adapts the language of paradigm while defining it more loosely than Kuhn’s usage for his account of changing American historiography.
edges.evidence_note: Own1989 note1 identifies The Structure of Scientific Revolutions(1962) and expressly limits paradigm here to a conceptual framework and/or its presuppositions. This records acknowledged terminology with an explicit departure, not adoption of Kuhn’s full theory or proof of a formative lineage. Kuhn’s original book unread.

edges.relationship: Higham draws on E. P. Thompson’s formulation of independent intellectual territory to explain why dissenting historians need a sustaining community.
edges.evidence_note: Own1989 printed462 names E.P.Thompson and quotes the need for journals and centers belonging to the community. This conceptual support sits within Higham’s argument about the isolation of radical scholarship; no organizational collaboration or exclusive influence is inferred. Note4 identifies Tocqueville for the preceding conformity argument and does not supply the Thompson source; its title/date remain unresolved and the original unread.

edges.relationship: Higham uses Black Reconstruction as an important example for distinguishing racial exclusion of a scholar from the uneven scholarly reception of radical historical work.
edges.evidence_note: Own1989 printed461/n3 ranks DuBois and Curti’s1935 works highly, describes white scholars’ use of DuBois’s evidence despite rejecting his Marxism, and makes that distinction part of his reply to Wiener. Higham’s account is attributed rather than independently certified;462 also makes an additional claim about DuBois’s lack of disciples, not independently verified here, which this edge does not adopt as fact or convert into a personal criticism. Curti, Beale and Armstead Robinson retain their separate credit; cited originals unread.

edges.relationship: Higham draws, through Ian Tyrrell’s account, on Genovese’s work as one example of the stronger interpretive resources of American radical scholarship in the1960s.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named mediation: Higham1989,461/n2 credits Ian Tyrrell’s The Absent Marx and names Genovese jointly with Gabriel Kolko and Barrington Moore,Jr. Higham says their example does not by itself explain the collective breakthrough. His465–466/n10 separately discusses Elkins and Tannenbaum as resources for Genovese and identifies The Political Economy of Slavery(1965). No sole-source lineage or fresh reading of Tyrrell/Genovese originals is claimed.

edges.relationship: Genovese credits Higham with encouraging Roll, Jordan, Roll when the project was still a two-page outline.
edges.evidence_note: Own reprinted acknowledgment specifically credits encouragement at an early outline stage. Adjacent manuscript editing and readers receive separate credit; Higham is not assigned those roles. The2011 digital preview reprints a1970s acknowledgment; no precise calendar year for encouragement is inferred from a decade ago, and the original1974 print edition is uncollated.

edges.relationship: Tosh acknowledges Davidoff’s jointly authored Family Fortunes as an inspiration and historical resource for the Manful Assertions project.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2023 retrospective p.178 and n.3 explicitly acknowledge both coauthors. The 2020 edited conversation, published 2023, pp.301–302 supplies a qualification: the group knew Family Fortunes but pursued men’s history as a totality and was less attentive than it could have been to multiple gender positions. This is a bounded debt for the shared 1991 project co-edited with Michael Roper; it is not sole authorship, complete adoption or a claim of chronological causal priority from co-presence.

edges.relationship: Tosh acknowledges Catherine Hall’s jointly authored Family Fortunes as an inspiration and historical resource for the Manful Assertions project.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2023 retrospective p.178 and n.3 explicitly acknowledge both coauthors. The 2020 edited conversation, published 2023, pp.301–302 supplies a qualification: the group knew Family Fortunes but pursued men’s history as a totality and was less attentive than it could have been to multiple gender positions. This is a bounded debt for the shared 1991 project co-edited with Michael Roper; it is not sole authorship, complete adoption or a claim of chronological causal priority from co-presence.

edges.relationship: Tosh draws on Foucault’s diagnosis of the present through the different world of the past to frame the public relevance of masculinity history.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2023 chapter pp.179–180 explains the diagnostic purpose of history of the present and its relevance to histories of masculine crises. It is a specific retrospective conceptual resource, with an immediately stated reservation, not proof of Tosh’s original formation. Note11 cites Discipline and Punish, Alan Sheridan translation, Vintage1995, pp.30–31; that translation is not independently read.

edges.relationship: Tosh questions the confinement of Foucault’s history of the present within academic discourse and proposes history for the present addressed to a lay public.
edges.evidence_note: Own chapter p.180: after recognizing Foucault’s relevance, Tosh states his reservation that Foucault did not consider reaching a lay readership and that subsequent practitioners seldom prioritize this. Criticism concerns public address, not a blanket rejection of genealogical analysis or a claim that Foucault wrote no public interventions. Foucault’s cited text remains mediated through Tosh’s stated reading.

edges.relationship: Tosh uses Scott’s claim that representations of the past construct gender in the present as a starting point for developing history addressed to lay audiences.
edges.evidence_note: Own chapter p.181 identifies Scott’s statement as foundational and then insists that productive public engagement requires more than the assumption: the priorities of lay readers may reset scholarly direction. The qualified use is retained in one resource edge; it establishes neither complete agreement nor a newly discovered original debt. Note14 identifies Gender and the Politics of History (1988), p.2; Scott’s book itself is not freshly read.

edges.relationship: Tosh invokes Davis’s call to study women and men within the whole system of gender relations to justify masculinity history as part of feminist inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh selected original-article opening p.179 read through Paperzz OCR, browser lines34–51. Tosh expressly identifies Davis’s 1975 response, interprets its relational power argument and makes the gendered study of men indispensable to feminist historical work. This is a demonstrated conceptual use, not merely a reference; the original Davis address remains unread and the OCR is not image-collated.

edges.relationship: Colley uses Hobsbawm’s account of national bonding against outsiders and his rejection of cultural homogeneity to frame British nation making.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary 1992 article opens with Hobsbawm’s1990 formulation p.309; more substantively p.316n. 18 identifies Hobsbawm pp.1–45 alongside Sahlins as the reasons for rejecting an integration/homogenization model. Colley then analyzes shared war,Protestantism and empire. This is a specific conceptual resource, not complete theoretical agreement or a claim to have freshly read Hobsbawm’s book.

edges.relationship: Colley takes up Pocock’s expanded British-history agenda and his account of Britain’s post-imperial relation to Europe.
edges.evidence_note: Primary pp.312–313 explains both the Four Nations gains and Pocock’s wider white-empire programme; p. 328 explicitly uses his observation that Britain can no longer control or avoid Europe,n. 53. Colley’s criticism of a narrowed Four Nations reception is not assigned to Pocock himself: she stresses that his original programme was geographically wider. UnderlyingPocock 1975/1982 articles unread.

edges.relationship: Colley uses Brewer’s account of war, fiscal bureaucracy and expanding armed forces to connect state formation with British national identification.
edges.evidence_note: Primary pp.321–322 explicitly says Brewer has shown how recurrent war strengthened the state; n. 36 identifies The Sinews of Power (1989). Colley distinguishes the established fiscal-military argument from her more tentative question about military service and popular solidarity, which she says is little researched. No automatic agreement on all dimensions and no fresh book reading.

edges.relationship: Colley draws on Said’s account of the Orient as Europe’s contrasting image to explain empire’s role in British self-definition.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primarypp.324–325 quotes and develops Said’s relation of Orient/West; nn. 45–46 identify Orientalism (1978), 1–2, 33–34. This is a specific resource in1992, compatible with her later particular objection about early British-Muslim relations as reported by Davis. Said’s whole book is not freshly read.

edges.relationship: Davis reports Colley’s objection that early British-Muslim captivity and commerce complicate a sequence from degrading stereotypes to imperial domination.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named mediation: Davis’s 2003 reviewsection 2,paragraph beginning Colley makes some interesting comparisons and following two paragraphs, explains her rejection of the relevant Said sequence: Islam was associated with threats to Britons, Catholic rivals were more immediate enemies, and commerce/scholarship made British discourse on Islam multifaceted. This bounded contextual objection is retained alongside her 1992 use of Said. Captives and Said originals unread; no claim to have independently adjudicated all Orientalism.

edges.relationship: As Breuilly explains, Colley uses Anderson’s imagined political community to treat Britain as an invented nation overlying older loyalties.
edges.evidence_note: Named scholarly mediation, Breuilly’s signed contribution acceptedpp.16–17 reproduces Colley’s 2003Pimlico wording and interprets the use. His qualification is essential: Colley moves from imagined community to invented nation and does not thereby adopt Anderson’s whole print-capitalism argument. Original1992and2003book bodies unread; no full-theory influence claim or claim based on citation frequency.

edges.relationship: Colley praises Pagden’s comparative study of imperial ideas but argues that commerce, conquest and global interaction exceed its Eurocentric account.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1996 review’s final Pagden section, especially final two paragraphs. She challenges exclusion of Dutch imperialism and the chronology of British militarism inIndia, then argues that wider global interactions are needed to explain continued conquests despite metropolitan criticism. Praise for innovative comparison and classical-ideology analysis coexists. Marshall’s separately reviewed collection is not confused with Pagden’s book; book itself unread.

edges.relationship: Pagden praises Captives but disputes Colley’s claim that the world remains imperial while becoming post-colonial.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2002 review final substantive objection and preceding praise. He argues that colonies persist while an empire requires incorporation and reciprocal cultural change, and that American global bases alone do not meet this definition. This remains Pagden’s dated 2002 judgment, not our current geographical or political classification,and is not proof of a direct reply to Colley’s 1996 review. Captives unread.

edges.relationship: Davis praises Captives while questioning its distinctions among forms of bondage, its treatment of the American Revolution and its emphasis on Britain’s smallness.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2003 review: section 2paragraphs beginning Colley should have done more and Professor Robert C. Davis distinguish slavery/captivity and warn against benign servitude; section 3 paragraph beginning While Colley succeeds challenges omission of Black revolutionary soldiers; final paragraph questions repeated smallness. His praise of complexity and Mediterranean chapters,and his earlier objection about omitted imperial legacies,remain explicit. These are David Brion Davis’s specific reservations,not neutral proof that Colley’s overall book is wrong. Robert C. Davis is a different cited scholar; no substitution. Book unread.

edges.relationship: Cozens reads Colley’s nation-in-arms argument as a challenge to Thompson’s class-centered account of working-class formation.
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly Cozens’s 2016 reconstruction pp.12–13: he describes an implicit double challenge,questioning representativeness of the industrial workers highlighted by Thompson and foregrounding common armed service/national culture. Hisp. 15 also records Colley’s concessions of uneven discontent and contested patriotism. Neither Britons nor The Making has been freshly read; Cozens cites Colley 2009 fourth edition (original 1992) and Thompson 1991 fourteenth edition (original 1963). Claim does not say Colley denies class or all conflict.

edges.relationship: Thompson questions whether volunteer evidence establishes Colley’s broad loyalist consensus and argues that national unity can coexist with class division.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh selected 1993 archival OCR includes skepticism about majority participation,volunteer humbug, and explicit compatibility of one British nation with two class nations; OCR snippets are reordered and not image-collated. Cozens 2016 pp.15–16,n. 32 independently reconstructs the precise volunteer-evidence and ambivalence objection,citing review p. 378. His explicit praise of Colley’s clear prose, stimulating study and exceptional illustrations is retained; no blanket rejection and no claim the whole original print review has been read.

edges.relationship: Colley includes Edmund Morgan among the scholars whose different historical fields broadened her outlook and prompted new topics.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2016 written interview opening global-outlook answer names Jonathan Spence, Edmund Morgan, John Blum and DavidBrion Davis,then explicitly credits learning from different scholars with new topic ideas. The individual edge retains that collective acknowledgment: it supplies no particular borrowed concept,sole influence or advisor claim. Demos’s subsequent lunch conversation—not this group as a whole—is the separately reported genesis of Captives. Shared Yale employment or friendship alone is not the basis.

edges.relationship: Colley includes David Brion Davis among the scholars whose different historical fields broadened her outlook and prompted new topics.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2016 written interview opening global-outlook answer names Jonathan Spence, Edmund Morgan, John Blum and DavidBrion Davis,then explicitly credits learning from different scholars with new topic ideas. The individual edge retains that collective acknowledgment: it supplies no particular borrowed concept,sole influence or advisor claim. edges.relationship: Gordon credits Alice Clark’s1919study with shaping her understanding of gender as a material practice.
edges.evidence_note: Own2006retrospective, Personal Anecdote, paragraph beginning with Clark’s Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century. Explicit book debt; not personal contact or a claim that the1919publication directly shaped her earlier Russian-history dissertation. Clark’s complete book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Gordon disputes Scott’s account of agency, defending action through unequal parties’ conflicts and a distinction between violence and its representations (1990).
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary continuationp853: Gordon retains social-control analysis while rejecting the interpretation of her argument she attributes to Scott. Page852 and the subsequent book-review exchange remain unread. This specific reply does not establish a blanket rejection of Scott or discourse analysis.

edges.relationship: Scott questions Gordon’s conception of agency in Heroes of Their Own Lives, proposing a discursive account rather than an autonomous individual attribute (1990).
edges.evidence_note: As reconstructed by Megan Clare Webber, introductionp7 and notes20–23, citing Scott’s reviewp851. The Scott original remains unread. A specific interpretive objection, not a claim that Scott denies historical action. Gordon’s separate reply is directly witnessed on853.

edges.relationship: Uses child-protection case records to reconstruct family power and negotiated social intervention, challenging the assumption of a formerly autonomous family (1983–84).
edges.evidence_note: Selected own article529–534: poor women and children can initiate outside intervention despite unequal power and real violence. This contributes to the family-history strand of the combined demography/family entry; it does not establish a demographic method or field foundation. Distinct from the existing women’s-history and Arizona racial-formation claims.

edges.relationship: Kerber uses Geertz’s account of common sense as culturally filled with presuppositions to explain the persuasive power of separate-spheres language.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 essay, 11/n2, quotes Local Knowledge (1983),84, in explaining how the trope shaped historians’ selections and readers’ expectations. This is a specific analytical resource, not adoption of Geertz’s entire anthropology or an exclusive formative influence. The cited original remains unread.

edges.relationship: Kerber draws on Arendt’s analysis of the Greek public/private distinction to extend the history of gendered spheres beyond nineteenth-century America.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 discussion, 18–19/n19, explicitly credits The Human Condition (1958),22–78, especially24/72, for the contrast between biological necessity and public action. Kerber examines a historically gendered exclusion; this does not endorse Greek prescriptions or Arendt’s complete political theory. Aristotle is separately cited through Benjamin Jowett’s translation, with Judith Hallett credited for that reference; Okin’s different resource remains separate. Originals unread.

edges.relationship: Kerber uses Hayden White’s warning about discourse exceeding its evidence to illuminate the ambiguity and historical usefulness of separate-spheres language.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed30/n41 links the trope’s hidden instrumentality and ambiguity to a substantial quotation from Tropics of Discourse (1978),1, on tensions between data and organizing consciousness. The named writer is Hayden White, not Deborah Gray White, who appears elsewhere in the essay. This specific rhetorical resource does not claim full agreement with White’s narrative theory; original unread.

edges.relationship: Kerber points to Scott’s analysis of gender as a resource for understanding political systems and gender relations as reciprocal social constructions.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 final paragraph and note55 identify Scott’s Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis (1986),1053–1075, as an especially valuable analysis for the argument. Montesquieu’s Persian Letters through C.J.Betts and Spirit of the Laws through Thomas Nugent, plus Michael Shapiro, receive their distinct credit. This does not infer Derrida’s or Lévi-Strauss’s personal influence from the essay’s generic deconstruction language. Scott’s original remains unread here.

edges.relationship: Kerber draws on Ryan’s account of family strategies and class formation to show how women’s separate sphere could support household mobility while limiting women’s own autonomy.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed24–25/n29 substantively discusses Cradle of the Middle Class (1981), especially56/185, in relation to paid women’s work, sons’ education and family interests. Printed37/n49 separately credits Ryan’s forthcoming urban-public-space work, without treating a later published version as already read; printed9 acknowledges Ryan’s counsel on drafts among many other readers. These specific uses do not establish exclusive influence, formal mentoring or agreement with every Ryan conclusion. Ryan originals and drafts unread.

edges.relationship: Kerber expressly credits Higginbotham’s interpretation of race as a resource for her discussion of Black women and the separate-spheres framework.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed26/n30 acknowledges an interpretive debt to Evelyn Brooks, The Problem of Race in Women’s History, alongside separately credited work by the Hortons, Sterling, Jones and Deborah Gray White. Higginbotham’s own Harvard CV establishes the identity through that distinctive chapter title and editor; metadata does not itself establish the debt. Kerber’s forthcoming volume title is preserved, not silently replaced with the later 1989 title. Printed9 also thanks Evelyn Brooks for counsel on earlier drafts, among many colleagues; no individual task or final chapter edition is inferred. Higginbotham chapter itself unread.

edges.relationship: Kerber credits Faust with counsel on earlier versions of her essay on separate-spheres rhetoric.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 author acknowledgment at9 names Drew Faust in a larger group of advisors. The credit concerns this particular essay’s earlier versions; it does not specify which passage Faust influenced, assign sole responsibility for a concept, establish formal mentoring or imply Faust endorsed all conclusions. Kerber retains responsibility for remaining errors. No independent manuscript correspondence read.

edges.relationship: Kerber uses Thompson’s account of industrial time discipline to distinguish changing work patterns among women and men.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed23 explicitly treats factory and school employment as entry into a clock-measured work regime given classic formulation by E.P.Thompson. Printed16/n14 supplies the 1967 essay citation and separately explains Cott’s extension to married women’s household tasks. The current Thompson-to-Cott edge2087 and Cott-to-Kerber edge2094 already record that distinct adaptation; this proposal concerns Kerber’s additional direct use in her comparison of women’s work regimes. Hareven and Dublin retain their separate empirical/interpretive credit; no fresh Thompson original or Cott book read.

edges.relationship: Kerber credits Hofstadter’s example with teaching her to ask consequential questions, choose her own research problem and connect historical understanding to political understanding.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2020 lecture2 and8 explains particular lessons, his readings seminar and approval of her dissertation prospectus. She also remembers his resistance to being called a consensus historian and his preference for skeptic, and says the book and conversation may have lodged in her thinking. Graduate peers share credit for the history/politics lesson; Lerner later supplied distinct mentoring after Hofstadter’s early death. This is explicit retrospective formation, not an inference solely from supervision or a claim that Hofstadter originated her later feminism. His original works and her dissertation unread.
